titulo.texto: Sculpture of the Huastec Adolescent of Tamuín

frase_gancho.texto: A young man of stone, engraved with maize, carrying a child on his back.

puente_narrativo.texto: From the young man of maize, we head north into Veracruz, where the Mexica empire also reached. Look for a stone stela with a standing god, wearing a tall cone-shaped headdress and a mask over his mouth.

guion_corto.texto: This young man of stone, more than a meter tall, comes from Tamuín, in San Luis Potosí, and is one of the most famous sculptures of the Huastec people. He stands slim and naked, his body upright and his head shaved. His left half is smooth, while the right is covered with engraved designs: maize plants and ears of corn, and heads of the wind god. It looks like a tattoo, or ritual paint, turned to stone. On his back he carries a small child. Is it the rising Sun? Is it tender young maize? Is it a deity? No one knows for certain. What we do see is a body that looks like a planted field.

guion_largo.texto:
Look closely at this body: it is a written page. What seems to be a simple naked young man is, in reality, a body covered in messages, and whoever knows how to read them will see the whole cycle of maize.

Start with the division. The left side is smooth and polished, almost without decoration. The right side, the arm, the leg and the back are covered with designs engraved in the stone. They look like tattoos, ornamental scars or ritual body paint. Remember the introductory hall: the body as a canvas, something the peoples of Mesoamerica took to many extremes. Here, the sculptor decided to show both states at once: the unadorned body and the body already clothed in symbols.

The designs are maize plants, ears of corn, symbols of the sky and heads of the wind god. In other words, this young man wears the field on his skin. It has been interpreted that he himself is the maize: slender, upright and tender, like a plant that sprouts. For the Huastecs, who lived from the milpa in a region of abundant rain, every little plant was a life, and the human body and the plant were almost the same thing.

And then there is the child he carries on his back. Who is it? Several ideas have been proposed. Perhaps the newborn Sun; perhaps the young maize; perhaps a deity. Some specialists link it to the wind god, Ehécatl-Quetzalcóatl, who swept the roads so that the rains would come, and whose emblem, the cut shell, he wears in the pond of the courtyard. There are those who see here the god himself, young, carrying the dawn of a new era. There is no single answer.

Now, an astonishing fact. The Huastecs speak Teenek, a language that belongs to the Maya family, even though they live more than a thousand kilometers from the Maya of the south, with many other peoples in between. Linguists think that, many centuries ago, a Maya-speaking group split from the rest and stayed in the north of the Gulf, where it kept its language and developed its own art. If you think about it, it is an enormous journey: a language that crossed the history of Mesoamerica without getting lost.

The Huastecs were great sculptors. Their stone figures tend to be frontal, with tall headdresses and solemn gestures, sometimes naked and with symbols of fertility. This one is among the most refined: the balance between the smooth part and the engraved part, and the delicacy of the outline, place it among the masterpieces of the museum.

Before moving on, look once more at the details. The face is serene, the arms rest on the chest and the belly, and the curved ear ornaments hang like small hooks. He is a young man, but also a plant, a day and a god. And all of it fits in a single stone.

One last detail: it is thought that this sculpture was part of a ceremonial space, and that it was not an ornament, but an image for the cult of fertility. In front of it, perhaps, people asked for rain and a good harvest. Today we ask for something simpler: that you pause for a moment to look at it.

texto.Origin: Consuelo site, Tamuín, San Luis Potosí
texto.Dimensions: 145 cm tall x 41 cm wide x 17.8 cm thick

texto.pregunta: Myth: The Huastecs were a Maya people, like those in the next hall.
texto.respuesta: Reality: They speak a language of the Maya family, but their culture, their art and their history developed separately, far from the Maya of the south.
